claims.text: Tribological performance of the HEA coating has a non-monotonic dependence on ambient temperature.
Wear resistance peaks in the intermediate range of 500–700 °C because of dynamic precipitation and dislocation forest hardening.
Above approximately 750 °C, dynamic recrystallization and grain-boundary sliding become dominant and accelerate wear.
The initial coating has a fine-grained microstructure.
Rapidly solidified CoCrFeMnNi can have a high initial dislocation density.
The initial coating may contain stabilized nanoscale Mn2O3 or carbide precipitates.
At 500–700 °C, stress-assisted dislocation climb is controlled by lattice diffusion.
Dynamic M23C6 carbides or Cr-rich sigma-phase precipitates form at intermediate temperatures.
The dynamic precipitates impede dislocation motion and increase the activation energy for deformation.
Above approximately 750 °C, thermal energy overcomes precipitate and grain-boundary pinning forces.
Exceeding approximately 750 °C triggers dynamic recrystallization and grain growth.
Dynamic recrystallization and grain growth reduce dislocation-forest and grain-boundary strengthening, softening the surface layer.
High-temperature softening changes the dominant wear mode from abrasive or adhesive wear to severe plastic deformation and material removal by grain-boundary sliding.
Specific wear rate decreases from room temperature to a minimum at approximately 600–700 °C.
Specific wear rate increases sharply above 750 °C.
Wear-scar morphology changes from shallow grooves at low temperature to deep plowing and delamination at high temperature.
At room temperature, deformation is dominated by slip and deformation twinning.
The room-temperature state has high yield strength associated with fine grains and high dislocation density.
The 750–800 °C range marks a transition from strain hardening to strain softening.
Peak-performance and degradation temperatures depend on HEA composition and precipitate identity.
